note.question: When can giving customers a credible opt-out choice increase a digital firm's profit as well as consumer and total welfare, and when does lost data revenue overturn those gains?
note.overview: A monopolistic digital firm chooses price anticipating heterogeneous consumers' purchase and data-sharing responses. The paper solves and compares firm-pricing and consumer-choice outcomes before and after the GDPR and derives profit, consumer-surplus, and total-surplus thresholds.

components.label: Model sequence and system structure
components.explanation: Consumers privately learn their types (v,c). The firm chooses service price p to maximize sales plus data-monetization revenue. Consumers then decide whether to buy; before the GDPR purchase entails data sharing, while after the GDPR buyers can choose opt-in or opt-out. Equilibrium outcomes under the two regimes are compared.
